title: How should you take notes during a case interview?
description: A practical way to lay out your paper in a case interview so you can find the goal, your structure and the numbers when you need them.
hook: Take notes on a fixed layout: the client's goal in a box at the top of page one with the key facts below it, your structure large on page two, and one page per calculation or chart after that. Write every number with its unit and keep updating the page as the case moves. Messy notes are behind many lost cases, because twenty minutes in you need the goal or a number and cannot find it.
body:
A layout that works

  • Page 1, top: the client's goal in a box, with its number and deadline: "Restore annual profit from $5M to $8M within two years."
  • Page 1, below: key facts from the prompt in short bullets. Circle anything surprising, and mark anything unclear with a question mark to ask about once the interviewer finishes.
  • Page 2: your structure, drawn large, landscape if it helps. Leave space under each branch to add findings later.
  • Page 3 onwards: one page per calculation or chart. Write the question at the top, then the working, then the answer with units, circled.

Bain's case interview guidance tells candidates to bring pen and paper, write clearly and be ready to walk the interviewer through their framework. A layout you use every time makes that easy. For what to capture while the prompt is read, see what to do while the interviewer reads the case.

Small habits that help

  • Write numbers with units: "$4.5M a year", not "4.5".
  • Use abbreviations you will recognise later: Rev, Cost, Cust, Mkt, Comp.
  • Mark which numbers the interviewer gave you and which are your own estimates.
  • Number your pages so you can say "on page two I noted..."
  • Turn the structure page towards the interviewer when you present it.

Update the page as the case moves

Notes should help you decide, not record everything. Suppose the goal is to take profit from $5M to $8M, a $3M gap, and you learn that revenue is flat while distribution costs rose $2M. Cross out the branches you have ruled out, and write one line of synthesis under your structure:

"Distribution explains two-thirds of the gap ($2M of $3M). Next: route density vs price per shipment."

At any point your notes should answer three questions: What is the client's goal? What have we established? What should we look at next? Those three lines are also the skeleton of your final recommendation.

For online interviews

You will usually still work on paper. McKinsey's advice for virtual interviews includes keeping pen and paper within reach. Bain suggests telling your interviewer when you are taking notes and describing your structure clearly, since they cannot see your page. Hold it up to the camera if that helps.

Test your notes

Practise with a recorded or partner-run case. Stop halfway and give a 30-second recap using only your page. If you cannot, your notes are either too detailed or not structured enough.

1. A prompt says: "Revenue $80M, down 10%; the CEO wants to return to last year's level within 18 months." What goes in the goal box?

Show the answer

"Revenue back to about $89M within 18 months." Last year's revenue was $80M ÷ 0.9 ≈ $88.9M, not $88M: the 10% fall was from the higher base, so you cannot just add 10% back.

2. Ten minutes in, you find a key number. Where does it go?

Show the answer

On the calculation page, circled with its unit, and as a one-line finding under the relevant branch of your structure, so you can find it again at the end.

Before the end

Glance at your goal box before you give your recommendation. It is the simplest way to make sure your answer matches the question that was actually asked. For the full opening routine, read how to open a case in the first two minutes, and practise on a case from the casebook.
